practice.stem: Which neurotransmitter is released by ALL autonomic preganglionic neurons?
options: Acetylcholine in the PNS, norepinephrine in the SNS
practice.rationale: "It's always acetylcholine from that first neuron" — both divisions release ACh onto Nn receptors at the ganglion. Norepinephrine is the SNS postganglionic transmitter, and epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla.

practice.stem: Which receptor is found at the skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction?
practice.rationale: N for nerve, M for muscle: Nm sits at the NMJ. Nn is at the autonomic ganglia; muscarinic receptors are on PNS target organs and sweat glands; α₁ is on smooth muscle.

practice.stem: Activation of α₂ receptors produces:
options: Decreased NE release and sympathetic outflow
practice.rationale: α₂ is the sympathetic system's negative feedback — "the brother that's always like, no, don't." Vasoconstriction is α₁, ↑ HR/contractility is β₁, bronchodilation is β₂.

practice.stem: Positive dromotropy from β₁ stimulation means:
options: Increased renin release from the kidney
Faster conduction through the AV junction
Faster heart rate from the SA node
practice.rationale: Dromotropy = conduction. Chronotropy (chrono = time) is rate, and inotropy is strength of contraction. Renin release is β₁'s kidney effect.

practice.stem: Sweat glands are the exception in autonomic wiring because they are:
options: Sympathetic, using norepinephrine at α₁ receptors
Sympathetic, but use ACh at muscarinic receptors
Parasympathetic, using ACh at muscarinic receptors
Innervated equally by both autonomic divisions
practice.rationale: Sweat glands are sympathetic, but the nerve releases ACh onto muscarinic receptors, so with drugs "sweating will follow the opposite of what you expect." The PNS has no significant sweat-gland innervation.

practice.stem: Which structure is innervated by only ONE division of the ANS?
practice.rationale: Blood vessels get essentially no parasympathetic input — "it's all sympathetic." The heart, bladder and eye have dual, opposed innervation.

practice.stem: Bethanechol's main therapeutic use is:
options: Urinary retention caused by an enlarged prostate
practice.rationale: Bethanechol makes the detrusor contract, so it's for a bladder that holds urine but can't contract — never when there's an obstruction. Atropine treats bradycardia; pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.

practice.stem: Pyridostigmine is used to treat:
practice.rationale: Pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor) keeps more ACh at the NMJ for myasthenia gravis. Neostigmine is the one that reverses nondepolarizing blockade; atropine treats cholinergic toxicity; dantrolene treats MH.

practice.stem: What is the antidote for malignant hyperthermia?
practice.rationale: Dantrolene is the MH antidote and must be rapidly available wherever triggering agents are used. Atropine treats cholinergic toxicity; neostigmine and pyridostigmine are AChE inhibitors.

practice.stem: Which is an EARLY clue of malignant hyperthermia?
practice.rationale: CO₂ reflects metabolism, so rising end-tidal CO₂ is "often the first sign"; hyperthermia may be a late sign. MH brings tachycardia and rigidity, not bradycardia or flaccidity.

practice.stem: Which drugs are nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers?
practice.rationale: Nondepolarizers "end in -curonium" and are Nm antagonists. Succinylcholine is the depolarizing agent; neostigmine and pyridostigmine are AChE inhibitors; bethanechol and atropine act at muscarinic receptors.

practice.stem: Clonidine (Catapres) is classified as a:
practice.rationale: Clonidine stimulates central presynaptic α₂ receptors to cut NE release. Prazosin is the α₁ antagonist, metoprolol the β₁-selective blocker, phenylephrine the selective α₁ agonist.

practice.stem: Which β-blocker is cardioselective (preferentially blocks β₁)?
practice.rationale: Metoprolol preferentially blocks β₁. Propranolol blocks β₁ + β₂, carvedilol blocks β₁ + β₂ + α₁, and prazosin isn't a β-blocker (α₁ antagonist).

practice.stem: Botulinum toxin works by:
options: Blocking Nm receptors at the NMJ
practice.rationale: Botulinum toxin acts at the presynaptic terminal so ACh never reaches the receptor. Blocking Nm is rocuronium/vecuronium; AChE inhibition is pyridostigmine/neostigmine; muscarinic activation is bethanechol.

practice.stem: An α₁ agonist causes vasoconstriction. What happens to blood pressure if a patient receives an α₁ antagonist?
options: BP falls because heart rate drops through β₁ blockade
BP is unchanged because the parasympathetic system takes over the vessels
practice.rationale: Blocking α₁ removes the signal to constrict, so vessels dilate and BP falls. Vessels have no parasympathetic input to "take over," and an α₁ blocker doesn't act on β₁.

practice.stem: A patient with urinary retention has a bethanechol order. Which finding should make the nurse hold the dose and contact the prescriber?
options: No void for 8 hours after surgery
A bladder scan showing a large volume of urine
A kidney stone lodged in the urethra
practice.rationale: "Make sure there's a place for the urine to go" — squeezing a bladder against an obstruction can rupture it. A full bladder and no void are why the drug is ordered; normal vitals aren't a reason to hold it.

practice.stem: A patient received atropine. Which assessment finding is an expected drug effect?
practice.rationale: Atropine = dry + fast + retention: tachycardia, dry mouth, mydriasis, constipation. Bradycardia, salivation, diarrhea and miosis are cholinergic effects — the opposite.

practice.stem: An 84-year-old taking several medications with anticholinergic properties becomes newly confused. The most likely explanation is:
practice.rationale: Older adults are "much more sensitive" to anticholinergics and the effects add up across drugs; confusion/agitation is a listed CNS effect. Cholinergic toxicity would bring SLUDGE signs instead.

practice.stem: A patient on pyridostigmine develops muscle twitching, drooling and diarrhea. The nurse suspects:
practice.rationale: Fasciculations ("twitches") plus salivation and diarrhea = too much ACh — "it may mean that we've given them too much." Anticholinergic toxicity would be dry, constipated and retaining.

practice.stem: Which drug should the nurse anticipate to treat dangerous muscarinic effects of cholinergic toxicity?
practice.rationale: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and is used to treat cholinergic toxicity. Neostigmine and bethanechol would add more cholinergic activity; dantrolene is for MH.

practice.stem: A ventilated ICU patient is receiving vecuronium and lies completely still. Which action is a priority?
options: Stop respiratory support as soon as the infusion is turned off
Skip eye care because the patient's eyes are closed by the drug
Confirm that sedation and analgesia are also being given
Decrease sedation because the paralytic keeps the patient calm
practice.rationale: PARALYSIS ≠ SEDATION ≠ ANALGESIA — a paralyzed patient can be awake and in pain. Paralyzed patients need eye/skin care, and recovery must be verified before respiratory support stops.

practice.stem: A patient on rocuronium is also started on gentamicin. What interaction should the nurse watch for?
practice.rationale: Aminoglycosides like gentamicin (along with general anesthetics and magnesium) can increase or prolong nondepolarizing blockade. MH and sux-type hyperkalemia belong to succinylcholine.

practice.stem: Why does neostigmine reverse rocuronium?
options: It blocks the muscarinic receptors instead
More ACh outcompetes the blocker at Nm
It speeds the breakdown of rocuronium
It directly stimulates the Nm receptors
practice.rationale: Neostigmine inhibits AChE, so ACh builds up and outcompetes the nondepolarizing blocker. It doesn't activate the receptor itself, and the muscarinic effects it causes are why an antimuscarinic is often given with it.

practice.stem: A patient with major burns from 3 weeks ago needs emergent intubation. Why is succinylcholine a concern?
options: Burns trigger malignant hyperthermia by themselves
Upregulated receptors → severe hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias
Burns make the patient resistant to all paralytics
Succinylcholine causes hypokalemia in burn patients
practice.rationale: After the acute phase, burns upregulate extrajunctional receptors — more channels open, more K⁺ leaves muscle, "their bodies are a little more primed." MH is genetic, triggered by sux or volatile anesthetics, not by burns.

practice.stem: After surgery with succinylcholine, a patient complains of diffuse muscle aches. The nurse explains this is because:
options: The drug's initial depolarization causes fasciculations
Malignant hyperthermia always causes mild muscle aches
The drug blocked Nm receptors without depolarizing them
practice.rationale: Sux is an Nm agonist — the initial depolarization causes brief fasciculations and postoperative muscle pain. Nondepolarizers don't depolarize, so they don't cause this.

practice.stem: A patient's BP rises from 84/50 to 150/92 on phenylephrine, and HR falls from 88 to 58. The best explanation is:
practice.rationale: Phenylephrine is a pure α₁ agonist: vasoconstriction raises BP, and the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart to compensate. It has no β₁-blocking or muscarinic action.

practice.stem: A patient has used albuterol many times a day for a week. Which lab value is most important to check?
options: Serum potassium, which may be low
Serum potassium, which may be high
practice.rationale: β₂ stimulation activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and shifts K⁺ into cells → hypokalemia, especially with higher systemic exposure. Hyperkalemia is the succinylcholine problem.

practice.stem: A patient taking clonidine says, "I feel dizzy, so I'm just going to stop it." The best response is:
options: "Don't stop suddenly — your BP can rebound high."
"Take a double dose tomorrow to make up for it."
"You can stop it whenever you like if you feel dizzy."
"Stopping it will make your blood pressure drop further."
practice.rationale: MAJOR SAFETY ISSUE: abrupt discontinuation → rebound sympathetic activity → severe hypertension, tachycardia, headache. It should be tapered; teach slow position changes for the dizziness.

practice.stem: A patient is starting prazosin for hypertension. Which instruction addresses its major safety concern?
options: Stop the drug if your nose feels stuffy
Take the first dose with breakfast so you can watch for side effects
Take the first dose at bedtime and rise slowly
Expect your heart rate to slow on the first dose
practice.rationale: First-dose effect: significant orthostatic hypotension/syncope after the initial dose, so the first dose is commonly given at bedtime with fall precautions. Reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia, may occur.

practice.stem: A patient with asthma needs a β-blocker. Which drug raises the greatest concern for bronchoconstriction?
practice.rationale: Propranolol blocks β₂, so its bronchoconstriction concern is "higher" (slide 72). Metoprolol's β₁ selectivity lowers the concern (though it isn't absolute); prazosin and clonidine don't block β receptors.

practice.stem: Patient on propranolol for migraine prevention is wheezing. Albuterol is given. Predict:
options: Bronchodilation may be weaker than expected
Bronchodilation will be stronger than usual
No interaction — the drugs act on different receptors
practice.rationale: Both act at β₂: propranolol blocks it and "can oppose β₂ agonists such as albuterol." They share a receptor, so there is an interaction.

practice.stem: Patient with HR 38 receives atropine. HR rises to 92. Mechanism:
options: Direct β₁ stimulation of the heart
Increased ACh acting at the SA node
practice.rationale: "Atropine does not directly stimulate the heart, it removes the parasympathetic 'brake'." More ACh would slow the heart further; α₁ acts on vessels.

practice.stem: Bethanechol given. Predict sweating:
options: Increased — sweat glands use muscarinic receptors
Decreased — the drug is parasympathetic and sweating is sympathetic
No change — the PNS doesn't innervate sweat glands
practice.rationale: A muscarinic agonist "doesn't care" who normally controls the gland — it finds the muscarinic receptor, so sweating increases. That's the sweat-gland exception.

practice.stem: Patient on atropine works outdoors on a hot afternoon. Predict:
practice.rationale: Blocking muscarinic receptors on sweat glands ↓ sweating, so the patient can't cool off — teach to avoid overheating. Atropine causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

practice.stem: Person with diabetes on metoprolol; blood glucose is low. Which sign is most likely still present?
practice.rationale: β-blockers blunt the adrenergic signs of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety), but sweating usually still occurs because sweat glands use ACh → muscarinic receptors.

practice.stem: Dobutamine started for low cardiac output in a patient with coronary disease. New chest pain. Why?
options: α₁ vasoconstriction of the coronary arteries
practice.rationale: Key concept: ↑ contractility = ↑ myocardial O₂ demand; angina is a listed adverse effect. Dobutamine is predominantly β₁, not α₁ or β₂, and it tends to raise HR, not lower it.

practice.stem: Norepinephrine infusing. IV site is swollen, cool and pale. Predict the risk:
practice.rationale: Norepinephrine is a powerful α₁ vasoconstrictor; extravasation causes local tissue injury/necrosis, which is why the IV site is monitored closely. This isn't a therapeutic effect.

practice.stem: Clonidine stopped abruptly 2 days ago. BP 190/110, HR 112, headache, nervous. Cause:
practice.rationale: Removing the α₂ "brake" suddenly → rebound sympathetic activity → severe hypertension, tachycardia, headache, nervousness. That's why clonidine is tapered.

practice.stem: Neostigmine given to reverse rocuronium. HR 52, copious secretions. Why?
options: The patient is developing malignant hyperthermia
Rocuronium is wearing off too fast
practice.rationale: AChE inhibitors raise ACh at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, so bradycardia and secretions are muscarinic effects — the reason an antimuscarinic is commonly coadministered.

practice.stem: Myasthenia gravis patient takes pyridostigmine. Predict muscle strength and GI motility:
practice.rationale: More ACh is available at both Nm (better NMJ transmission in MG) and muscarinic receptors (↑ GI motility, cramping, diarrhea as adverse effects).

practice.stem: Tamsulosin started for BPH. Patient stands up quickly from bed. Predict:
practice.rationale: α₁A blockade relaxes prostate/bladder-neck smooth muscle, but dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are its main adverse effects — teach slow position changes. It improves urine flow and doesn't touch β₂.

practice.stem: Anaphylaxis: wheezing, BP 76/40. Epinephrine IM. Which receptor relieves the wheezing?
practice.rationale: β₂ → bronchodilation → improved airflow. α₁ raises BP and reduces mucosal edema; β₁ raises HR and contractility; α₂ isn't part of the anaphylaxis benefit.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Post-op surgical unit
clinical.text: A 67-year-old woman is 2 days after abdominal surgery. She has not voided for 9 hours and says she feels the urge but "nothing comes." Bladder scan: large volume of retained urine. The surgeon writes an order for bethanechol. Vitals: BP 124/72, HR 78, RR 16, SpO₂ 97% on room air.

questions.stem: Before giving the first dose, what must the nurse make sure of?
options: That she has eaten a full meal beforehand
That an anticholinergic was given first
That her heart rate is above 100 beats/min
That there is no urinary or GI obstruction
questions.rationale: "Before making the bladder contract harder, make sure it has a route for urine to get out" — a stuck stone or bowel obstruction can lead to rupture. The drug is given on an empty stomach, and no anticholinergic pre-dose is needed.

questions.stem: Which findings are expected adverse effects of bethanechol? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Adverse effects follow excess muscarinic activity: bradycardia, cramping/diarrhea, salivation, sweating, urinary urgency. Dry mouth and retention are anticholinergic — "all going to be opposite."

questions.stem: How should the nurse give bethanechol?
options: Only at bedtime, because of dizziness
With a large meal, to protect the stomach
questions.rationale: The slide says it's often given on an empty stomach to reduce nausea/vomiting. Bedtime dosing is the prazosin first-dose rule.

questions.stem: An hour later her HR is 46, she is wheezing and sweating heavily. Which drug should the nurse anticipate?
questions.rationale: Severe cholinergic effects are opposed by an antimuscarinic such as atropine. Neostigmine and more bethanechol would add cholinergic activity; phenylephrine is an α₁ vasopressor.

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Emergency department
clinical.text: A 72-year-old man arrives dizzy and pale after nearly fainting at home. Vitals: HR 38, BP 82/48, RR 18, SpO₂ 95%. The provider orders atropine IV. History: hypertension, and he mentions an eye doctor once told him he has "narrow angles."

questions.stem: How does atropine raise his heart rate?
options: It blocks muscarinic receptors (removes the brake)
It causes vasoconstriction through α₁ receptors
It directly stimulates β₁ receptors in the heart
It increases ACh at the SA node
questions.rationale: "We're not directly stimulating the heart, but we're removing the brake." Muscarinic activity normally slows the heart; blocking it lets HR rise.

questions.stem: Which part of his history should the nurse report before atropine is repeated?
questions.rationale: Antimuscarinic effects can worsen narrow-angle glaucoma (slide 32 precautions). The near-fainting and pallor are why he needs treatment.

questions.stem: After atropine, his HR is 96. Which new finding is expected from the drug?
questions.rationale: Dry + fast + retention: atropine brings dry mouth and mydriasis. Salivation, miosis, diarrhea and sweating are cholinergic effects.

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Long-term care
clinical.text: An 84-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia lives in long-term care. His medication list includes three drugs with anticholinergic properties. Today staff report he is newly confused and agitated. He has had no bowel movement in 4 days, his bladder is distended, his mouth is very dry, and his temperature is 100.6°F after an afternoon sitting in a sunny courtyard.

questions.stem: Which of his findings are consistent with anticholinergic effects? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Anticholinergic effects: CNS confusion (especially in older adults), constipation, urinary retention, dry mouth, ↓ sweating with heat intolerance. Diarrhea and miosis are cholinergic.

questions.stem: Why is he at particular risk?
options: His BPH makes him sweat more than usual
Older adults break down acetylcholine faster
Older adults are more sensitive, and effects add up
questions.rationale: Older adults are "much more sensitive to anticholinergic drugs," and other drugs with anticholinergic properties increase the risk — a cumulative burden.

questions.stem: How does his BPH interact with these medications?
options: BPH protects him from urinary retention
Anticholinergics can worsen his urinary retention
questions.rationale: Urinary retention/BPH is a listed precaution — blocking muscarinic receptors reduces bladder emptying on top of the prostate's obstruction.

questions.stem: Which nursing action best addresses the cause?
options: Encourage more time outdoors in the sunny courtyard
Review Rx and OTC drugs for anticholinergic effects
Give atropine to treat the agitation
Restrict fluids to prevent bladder distention
questions.rationale: Slide 32: review prescription and OTC medications for anticholinergic effects; also avoid overheating and encourage hydration. Anticholinergics are on the Beers list for adults over 65. Atropine would add to the burden.

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Neurology clinic → ED
clinical.setting: Outpatient neuro follow-up, then ED the same evening
clinical.text: A 41-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis takes pyridostigmine. She took extra doses this week because her eyelids were drooping. In the ED she has drooling, watery eyes, frequent urination, diarrhea and vomiting, and visible muscle twitching. Vitals: HR 50, BP 98/60, RR 22, SpO₂ 93%.

questions.stem: Which of her findings suggest excessive cholinergic activity? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: SLUDGE — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis — plus bradycardia. Dry mouth and tachycardia point the other way (anticholinergic).

questions.stem: Her twitching is followed by increasing weakness. What does this sequence mean?
options: Twitching is an expected, harmless effect
The pyridostigmine dose is wearing off
questions.rationale: Excess nicotinic stimulation: fasciculations → weakness → paralysis. "If we start seeing any weird muscle twitching… it may mean that we've given them too much."

questions.stem: Which assessment is the priority?
questions.rationale: With MG, monitor muscle strength and respiratory function; RR 22 and SpO₂ 93% with rising weakness threaten breathing.

questions.stem: Which medication should the nurse anticipate for the dangerous muscarinic effects?
questions.rationale: Atropine treats cholinergic toxicity by blocking muscarinic receptors. Neostigmine and bethanechol would add cholinergic activity.

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Intensive care unit
clinical.text: A 58-year-old man with severe respiratory failure is intubated and on a ventilator. Because he keeps fighting the ventilator, he is started on a rocuronium infusion. He now lies completely still with no purposeful movement. His eyes are partly open.

questions.stem: His family asks, "He looks peaceful — does that mean he's asleep and comfortable?" The best response:
options: "He doesn't need other medicines while on this drug."
"Yes, he can't feel anything while he can't move."
"No — he also needs medicines for sedation and pain."
"Yes, the paralytic keeps him asleep and calm."
questions.rationale: PARALYSIS ≠ SEDATION ≠ ANALGESIA — blockers provide no unconsciousness, sedation or pain relief, so patients need additional medications.

questions.stem: Which actions belong in his care plan? Select all that apply.
options: Remove ventilatory support as soon as the infusion stops
Ensure sedation and analgesia are given
Eye care to protect the corneas
Monitor the degree of blockade with peripheral nerve stimulation
Hold analgesia because he shows no signs of pain
questions.rationale: Paralyzed patients need eye, skin and positioning care, sedation and analgesia, and monitoring of blockade depth (train-of-four). He can't show pain, and recovery must be verified before respiratory support stops.

questions.stem: The team decides to stop the blockade. Neostigmine is ordered. How does it work?
options: More ACh outcompetes rocuronium at Nm receptors
It directly stimulates the Nm receptors
It binds rocuronium and inactivates it
questions.rationale: Neostigmine ↓ ACh breakdown → ↑ ACh at the NMJ → ACh competes more effectively with the blocker for Nm receptors.

questions.stem: What must the nurse confirm before respiratory support is discontinued?
options: That he received a second paralytic dose
That his HR is below 60 beats/min
That sedation has been off for 24 hours
questions.rationale: Verify adequate recovery before discontinuing respiratory support — "make sure that the patient can breathe before we pull that tube out."

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — ED rapid-sequence intubation
clinical.text: A 34-year-old man was treated for major burns 2 weeks ago and is now back in the ED with worsening respiratory distress. The team needs to intubate quickly. Someone suggests succinylcholine because it is fast; another suggests rocuronium.

questions.stem: Why is succinylcholine risky for this patient?
options: He is too young for succinylcholine
Burns make him resistant to succinylcholine
questions.rationale: Major burns after the acute phase upregulate extrajunctional ACh receptors → more K⁺ efflux during depolarization → severe hyperkalemia → dysrhythmias.

questions.stem: Which other conditions carry the same succinylcholine hyperkalemia risk? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Slide 44's list: major burns after the acute phase, major crush injury/trauma, spinal cord injury, denervation, prolonged immobilization, certain neuromuscular disorders.

questions.stem: Why is succinylcholine often chosen in emergencies?
options: It is easily reversed by neostigmine
It provides sedation as well as paralysis
questions.rationale: It's used when rapid airway control/intubation is needed — "this one is a lot faster, so especially in emergency situations." It still paralyzes the respiratory muscles and gives no sedation.

questions.stem: How does succinylcholine produce paralysis?
options: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the NMJ
It blocks ACh binding without depolarizing
questions.rationale: Sux binds Nm, depolarizes and keeps it depolarized → flaccid paralysis. Blocking without depolarizing is rocuronium; preventing release is botulinum toxin.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Operating room → PACU
clinical.setting: OR, general anesthesia with a volatile agent
clinical.text: A 22-year-old man is having knee surgery under general anesthesia with a volatile inhaled anesthetic; succinylcholine was used for intubation. Twenty minutes in, the end-tidal CO₂ is rising rapidly and his jaw and limbs are rigid. HR 132. Temperature is still 37.8°C. Afterward his mother says her brother "had a bad reaction to anesthesia once."

questions.stem: What is the most likely problem?
questions.rationale: Sux plus a volatile anesthetic in a genetically susceptible person → MH: rapidly rising end-tidal CO₂ and rigidity are the early clues.

questions.stem: Why is his temperature only slightly raised?
options: The anesthetic keeps his temperature down permanently
Hyperthermia is a late sign; CO₂ rises first
questions.rationale: "It's like carbon dioxide that is often the first sign" — CO₂ reflects metabolism; temperature climbs later (to "105, 106 degrees").

questions.stem: Put these MH actions in priority order.
options: Give dantrolene and start supportive cooling
Keep monitoring cardiovascular and respiratory status
Recognize the early signs: rapidly rising end-tidal CO₂ and rigidity
questions.rationale: Recognize early signs → stop triggers → dantrolene (antidote) with supportive care such as ice and cooling blankets → ongoing CV/respiratory monitoring.

questions.stem: Which findings fit malignant hyperthermia? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Abnormal Ca²⁺ release → sustained muscle activity and hypermetabolism → rapid ↑ CO₂, rigidity, tachycardia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, rising temperature.

questions.stem: What does his mother's comment mean for future surgeries?
options: It only matters if he ever has local anesthesia
He should receive extra succinylcholine next time
Family history of MH — avoid or use extreme caution with sux
It is unrelated, since MH isn't inherited in families
questions.rationale: MH is pharmacogenetic; personal/family history is a contraindication. That's why patients are asked whether anyone in the family had a bad reaction to anesthesia.

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Botox clinic → ED
clinical.setting: ED visit 5 days after an outpatient procedure
clinical.text: A 45-year-old woman received botulinum toxin injections for chronic migraine 5 days ago. Today she reports trouble swallowing, generalized weakness and feeling short of breath. Vitals: HR 96, RR 24, SpO₂ 92%.

questions.stem: How does botulinum toxin work?
questions.rationale: Botulinum toxin prevents presynaptic ACh release, so ACh can't reach cholinergic receptors → ↓ muscle contraction/cholinergic activity.

questions.stem: What do her symptoms suggest?
options: An expected local effect needing no follow-up
Rare systemic spread of the toxin
questions.rationale: Adverse effects are usually local weakness, but rare systemic spread can cause generalized weakness, dysphagia and respiratory compromise — "the absolute worst case scenario."

questions.stem: Which drug in her history would most add to the weakness?
options: A β₂ agonist inhaler for asthma
A muscarinic agonist for urinary retention
An α₁ blocker taken for blood pressure
questions.rationale: Drug interaction concept: other medications that impair neuromuscular transmission may increase weakness.

questions.stem: Her friend uses botulinum toxin for excessive underarm sweating. Why does it work?
options: Sweat glands run on ACh at muscarinic receptors
It stimulates norepinephrine release in the skin
It blocks α₁ receptors on the sweat glands
Sweat glands are controlled by the parasympathetic system
questions.rationale: Even though sweating is sympathetic, the glands run on ACh at muscarinic receptors — so cutting ACh release treats hyperhidrosis.

clinical.title: Scenario 9 — Emergency department
clinical.text: A 19-year-old college student ate a cookie containing peanuts 15 minutes ago. She has hives, swollen lips, wheezing and a hoarse voice. Vitals: BP 78/40, HR 128, RR 28, SpO₂ 90%. She has an epinephrine autoinjector but didn't use it.

questions.stem: What causes her hypotension and swelling?
options: Excess α₁ stimulation of the vessels
questions.rationale: In anaphylaxis, mediators cause vasodilation + ↑ permeability → hypotension and tissue edema, plus bronchoconstriction and airway edema → impaired ventilation.

questions.stem: How should the nurse give epinephrine for anaphylaxis?
questions.rationale: Slide 54 nursing implication: for anaphylaxis, IM administration in the anterolateral thigh.

questions.stem: Which receptor effects of epinephrine help her? Select all that apply.
options: α₁ → vasoconstriction raises BP and reduces mucosal edema
questions.rationale: Epinephrine hits everything: α₁ ↑ BP and ↓ mucosal edema, β₁ cardiac stimulation, β₂ bronchodilation — the "ideal receptor profile for anaphylaxis." Muscarinic stimulation causes bronchoconstriction; α₂ activation decreases NE release.

questions.stem: Her HR is 128 and she has a history of palpitations. Is epinephrine contraindicated?
options: Only if her systolic BP is above 90 mm Hg
Yes — tachycardia is an absolute contraindication
Yes — give phenylephrine instead of epinephrine
No — anaphylaxis has no absolute contraindication
questions.rationale: "In a life-threatening emergency such as anaphylaxis, there is no absolute contraindication." Caution with CV disease applies to other settings; monitor HR, BP and rhythm.

questions.stem: Put these events in order, from exposure to epinephrine's effect.
options: Epinephrine α₁ vasoconstriction raises BP and reduces mucosal edema
questions.rationale: Mediator release → vasodilation + ↑ permeability → hypotension + tissue edema; epinephrine's α₁ effect reverses it (↑ BP, ↓ mucosal edema).

questions.stem: Before discharge, which teaching is most important?
options: Use the autoinjector only if hives spread to the legs
Correct autoinjector use + ED evaluation after any use
No follow-up is needed once the autoinjector is used
Inject it into a vein for a faster effect
questions.rationale: Teach patients with autoinjectors correct use and the need for emergency evaluation after administration.

clinical.title: Scenario 10 — ICU, septic shock
clinical.text: A 66-year-old woman with septic shock remains hypotensive. The provider starts a norepinephrine (Levophed) infusion titrated to a prescribed BP target. Vitals on start: BP 78/42, HR 118, warm skin, urine output low.

questions.stem: Why does norepinephrine fit septic shock?
options: It lowers heart rate through α₂ receptors
It is a pure β₂ agonist that dilates the bronchi
questions.rationale: Norepinephrine is strong α₁ (some β₁) → vasoconstriction → ↑ SVR → ↑ BP; especially important in distributive/septic shock where vasodilation is a major cause.

questions.stem: A resident asks whether the norepinephrine means no more IV fluids are needed. The nurse knows:
options: No — fluids are contraindicated with vasopressors
Yes — more fluids would reverse norepinephrine
Yes — norepinephrine replaces the lost volume
questions.rationale: Precaution: hypovolemia should be recognized and addressed, because vasoconstriction does not replace adequate circulating volume.

questions.stem: Two hours later the IV site is swollen, cool and pale. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Extravasation → local tissue injury/necrosis; that's why the IV site is monitored closely.

questions.stem: Her BP is now above target and her fingers are cool and dusky. What is the concern?
options: Muscarinic stimulation of the skin vessels
An expected and desirable drug effect
questions.rationale: Excessive vasoconstriction ↓ peripheral perfusion and causes ischemia; assess perfusion and titrate to the prescribed target.

questions.stem: Later she is switched to phenylephrine. BP rises to 132/80 and HR falls from 110 to 62. Why?
options: Her sepsis has resolved, so HR normalized
questions.rationale: Phenylephrine is pure α₁: BP rises and the baroreceptors slow the heart — reflex bradycardia is a listed adverse effect.

clinical.title: Scenario 11 — Cardiac step-down unit
clinical.text: A 70-year-old man with heart failure and coronary artery disease has signs of low cardiac output: cool extremities, low urine output, BP 92/58. He takes metoprolol at home. The team starts a dobutamine infusion. Vitals: HR 88, RR 20.

questions.stem: What is the goal of dobutamine?
options: Slowing the heart rate to rest the heart
questions.rationale: Dobutamine is predominantly β₁: ↑ myocardial contractility → ↑ SV → ↑ CO (it may also raise HR).

questions.stem: Thirty minutes later HR is 118 and he reports chest pressure. The explanation:
questions.rationale: ↑ contractility = ↑ myocardial O₂ demand; tachycardia and angina are listed adverse effects — use caution in ischemic heart disease; monitor HR/rhythm and chest pain.

questions.stem: How might his home metoprolol affect the dobutamine?
options: β-blockers may reduce dobutamine's β₁ effects
questions.rationale: Both act at β₁ — β-blockers may reduce its β₁-mediated effects.

questions.stem: He is discharged on carvedilol. Which teaching is correct? Select all that apply.
options: Expect slower heart rate and check HR/BP as instructed
Skip doses on days you feel dizzy
It only affects the heart, so it can't affect breathing
Rise slowly if you feel dizzy
Report worsening heart-failure symptoms when the dose is started or changed
questions.rationale: Carvedilol: orthostatic hypotension (rise slowly), do not stop abruptly, watch for worsening HF when started/titrated, monitor HR and BP. It blocks β₂ too, so bronchospasm risk exists.

questions.stem: Why does carvedilol cause more orthostatic hypotension than metoprolol?
options: It acts as a β₂ agonist in vessels
questions.rationale: Carvedilol blocks β₁ + β₂ + α₁; α₁ blockade → vasodilation → ↓ SVR. Metoprolol is β₁-selective with no α₁ effect.

clinical.title: Scenario 12 — Rapid rounds
clinical.setting: Primary care and pulmonary clinic, one quick patient at a time
clinical.text: Six patients, one question each. Use the receptor, then predict the drug effect.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with asthma needs a β-blocker for another condition. Which choice raises the greater bronchospasm concern?
questions.rationale: Propranolol blocks β₂ ("higher" bronchoconstriction concern); metoprolol is β₁-preferring ("lower"), though selectivity isn't absolute.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has used albuterol 8 times a day this week and has a fine tremor. What does the frequent use suggest?
options: Albuterol is a maintenance drug and this is normal
The asthma is not adequately controlled
The tremor means albuterol has stopped working
questions.rationale: Frequent need for rescue medication may indicate inadequate disease control. Tremor is a listed albuterol effect; check K⁺ too.

questions.stem: A person with type 1 diabetes takes propranolol. Which hypoglycemia sign is most likely to still appear?
questions.rationale: β-blockers blunt tachycardia, tremor and anxiety, but sweating usually still occurs because sweat glands use ACh → muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A patient ran out of clonidine 2 days ago. BP 188/108, HR 110, pounding headache. Cause?
questions.rationale: Sudden discontinuation → rebound sympathetic activity → severe HTN, tachycardia, headache, nervousness. Taper rather than stop.

questions.stem: A patient is starting prazosin. When should the first dose be taken?
questions.rationale: First-dose effect (orthostatic hypotension/syncope) — the initial dose is commonly given at bedtime.

questions.stem: A man with BPH starting tamsulosin asks, "Will this shrink my prostate?"
options: No — it improves flow but doesn't shrink it
Yes — it shrinks the prostate within a week
No — it only lowers your blood pressure
Yes — it shrinks it by blocking β₂ receptors
questions.rationale: Teach that tamsulosin improves urinary flow but does not eliminate the underlying prostate enlargement.

qa.q: Piloerection — which is the fancy name for…?
qa.a: Goosebumps (the class answered) — "you get to look bigger."

qa.q: (student asked) Are Nn and Nm both ion channels?
qa.a: Yes — both ion channels: we want a fast muscle response and fast transfer between neurons. Follow-ups weren't audible; she added that muscarinic receptors are the ones at the parasympathetic target organs, and the second diagram shows the same thing.

qa.q: If an α₁ agonist causes vasoconstriction, what would happen if we gave an α₁ antagonist?
qa.a: Vasodilation → ↓ BP — "good."

qa.q: If an α₁ agonist causes contraction of the prostate and bladder smooth muscle, what would happen if we gave an α₁ antagonist?
qa.a: Relaxation → improved urine flow. "Opposite side of the coin for almost everything except for sweat."

qa.q: (student asked) [mostly inaudible — about epinephrine vs norepinephrine at these receptors]
qa.a: They bind with different strengths, "a little beyond where I need you to be" — learn the receptor first, then match drugs to it.

qa.q: (student asked) [about what α₂ activation does / is used for]
qa.a: ↓ BP — it tells NE-releasing cells to "slow down a little"; also an adjunct for ADHD, PTSD and other off-label uses. Less heart rate, lower BP. (α₂ agonist — slide 19)

qa.q: (student asked) Does blocking just remove the brake — would it have the opposite effect?
qa.a: "Exactly." It depends on the drug, but vessels have no parasympathetic input, so pulling back the sympathetic → vasodilation.

qa.q: (student asked) So an α₂ antagonist would do the opposite?
qa.a: "Theoretically yes, but we don't have any drugs that do that." (slide 73: ↑ NE release*)

qa.q: Predict: stimulate α₁ → BP? β₁ → HR and contractility? β₂ → bronchi? Muscarinic → GI motility and bladder emptying?
qa.a: BP ↑ (from slide 18) · HR/contractility up · bronchi dilate (from slide 21) · muscarinic → "more, yes, more of that." (Her "predict the response" slide isn't in the posted deck — guided notes ¶40–47.)

qa.q: Now block them: α₁ → BP? β₁ → contractility? β₂ → bronchi? Muscarinic → GI and bladder?
qa.a: BP ↓ (from slide 18) · contractility down · bronchi constrict — "some good and bad things" · GI/bladder ↓ (from slide 73).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which neurotransmitter is released by all ANS preganglionic neurons?
qa.a: Acetylcholine — "it's always acetylcholine from that first neuron."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which receptor is found at the skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction?
qa.a: Nicotinic M (muscle).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Stimulation of α₁ receptors produces which effect?
qa.a: Vasoconstriction → ↑ BP (from slide 18) — α₁ is mainly on the vasculature, and "we manipulate them a lot when we're talking about blood pressure."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which effect is expected with β₁ receptor stimulation?
qa.a: ↑ HR and contractility — "one heart."

qa.q: (Kahoot) β₂ receptor stimulation produces which pulmonary effect?
qa.a: Bronchodilation — "if I'm running away from a bear… getting more air into my lungs."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Activation of α₂ receptors has which effect?
qa.a: ↓ NE release / ↓ sympathetic outflow (from slide 19) — "our negative feedback that keeps everything in check."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which response is caused by muscarinic receptor stimulation?
qa.a: Exact option not audible — "anything that the parasympathetic nervous system does" (from slide 22: e.g., ↓ HR, miosis, ↑ GI motility, bladder emptying, ↑ salivation).

qa.q: (Kahoot) A sudden medication-induced rise in blood pressure may trigger which response?
qa.a: Reflex bradycardia — reflex tachycardia is the opposite case, when BP falls.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Bethanechol is most appropriate for which condition?
qa.a: Nonobstructive urinary retention — "if we did have that block… we would risk potentially causing bladder rupture."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding is an expected adverse effect of bethanechol?
qa.a: Answer not audible — a cholinergic effect (from slide 30: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchoconstriction, diarrhea, salivation, sweating, urinary urgency). Her hint: the anticholinergic options (urinary retention, dry mouth) "are all going to be opposite."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Atropine produces which effect?
qa.a: Urinary retention.

qa.q: (Kahoot) How does pyridostigmine improve myasthenia gravis?
qa.a: It's an AChE inhibitor — blocks the breakdown of ACh, so more ACh at the neuromuscular junction.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding best suggests excessive cholinergic activity?
qa.a: A SLUDGE finding — "we got the S in there and the D."

qa.q: (student asked) Do nurses need someone to cosign for medications like these?
qa.a: Cosigning is mostly for wasting narcotics (e.g., a 5 mg dose from a 10 mg vial); she didn't think neuromuscular blockers require it. The Vanderbilt case involved multiple failures.
